title: How many hours of training does a nurse aide need under federal rules?
description: Federal nurse aide rules: 75 clock hours with 16 supervised practical hours (42 CFR 483.152), the 483.154 competency evaluation, and the 24-month lapse rule.
shortAnswer: A state-approved nurse aide training and competency evaluation program must run at least 75 clock hours, including at least 16 hours of supervised practical training and 16 hours of listed topics before any resident contact, under 42 CFR 483.152. The aide must then pass a written or oral test and a skills demonstration under 483.154. A nursing home may not use an aide for more than 4 months unless qualified, and 24 months without paid nursing work requires retraining.
keyTakeaways: 75 clock hours is the federal minimum for a state-approved program, with at least 16 hours of supervised practical training under a registered or licensed practical nurse.

Sixteen hours on communication, infection control, safety and emergency procedures including the Heimlich maneuver, residents' independence and residents' rights must come before any direct contact with a resident.

The competency evaluation has two parts, a written or oral examination and a skills demonstration, and the skills part is run by a registered nurse with at least one year of experience caring for the elderly or chronically ill.
Under 42 CFR 483.35(d)(6), 24 consecutive months without paid nursing or nursing-related services means a new training and competency evaluation program or a new competency evaluation.
Aides employed or offered employment by a facility when they start a program may not be charged for any part of it, including textbooks.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state approval and registries)
regulator: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), US Department of Health and Human Services, with State survey agencies
appliesTo: Skilled nursing facilities (Medicare) and nursing facilities (Medicaid) using nurse aides
Nurse aide training and competency evaluation programs (NATCEPs) and competency evaluation programs (CEPs) seeking state approval
Individuals training or testing as nurse aides, including temporary, per diem and agency aides

sections.heading: How do the federal nurse aide rules fit together?

blocks.text: They split into facility duties and program standards. [42 CFR 483.35(d)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-483/subpart-B/section-483.35) tells a nursing home whom it may use as a nurse aide. Subpart D, [42 CFR 483.151](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-483/subpart-D/section-483.151) to 483.156, tells states which training programs and competency evaluations they may approve and how the nurse aide registry works. Ongoing in-service training for employed aides sits in 483.95(g) and is covered on the [CMS nursing home training requirements page](/regulations/cms-nursing-home-training-requirements).

Older materials sometimes cite the facility duties under a different paragraph number. Since CMS reorganized the long-term care requirements, the hiring, registry and retraining rules are in 483.35(d). This page states the federal floor as at November 2026 from eCFR text current to November 5, 2026; many states require more than 75 hours.

sections.heading: What must a nurse aide training program include?

blocks.text: At least 75 clock hours of training, at least 16 hours of supervised practical training, and a defined curriculum. Under [42 CFR 483.152(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-483/subpart-D/section-483.152), supervised practical training means training in a laboratory or other setting where the trainee demonstrates knowledge while performing tasks on an individual under the direct supervision of a registered nurse or licensed practical nurse.

blocks.title: 42 CFR 483.152(b)(1): before any resident contact
blocks.text: At least a total of 16 hours of training in communication and interpersonal skills; infection control; safety and emergency procedures, including the Heimlich maneuver; promoting residents' independence; and respecting residents' rights, "prior to any direct contact with a resident."

The rest of the curriculum under 483.152(b) covers basic nursing skills (vital signs, height and weight, the resident's environment, recognizing and reporting abnormal changes, care when death is imminent), personal care skills (bathing, grooming including mouth care, dressing, toileting, eating and hydration, feeding techniques, skin care, transfers, positioning and turning), mental health and social service needs, care of cognitively impaired residents including dementia, basic restorative services, and residents' rights including freedom from abuse and avoiding restraints.

Students may not perform any service they have not been trained in and found proficient at by the instructor, and students providing services to residents must be under the general supervision of a licensed or registered nurse.

sections.heading: Who may teach nurse aide training?

blocks.text: Training must be performed by, or under the general supervision of, a registered nurse with at least 2 years of nursing experience, at least 1 year of which is in long term care facility services. Instructors must also have completed a course in teaching adults or have experience teaching adults or supervising nurse aides.

In a facility-based program, the director of nursing may provide general supervision but is prohibited from performing the actual training. Other health professionals, from pharmacists and dietitians to fire safety experts and resident rights experts, may supplement the instructor if they have at least 1 year of experience in their fields.

sections.heading: How is a nurse aide's competency evaluated?

blocks.text: By a two-part evaluation under [42 CFR 483.154](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-483/subpart-D/section-483.154): a written or oral examination and a skills demonstration. The aide chooses written or oral. The examination must address every course requirement in 483.152(b), be drawn from a pool of questions only part of which is used in any one test, and be protected against disclosure.

items: The skills demonstration uses randomly selected items from a pool of tasks generally performed by nurse aides, and the pool must include all personal care skills in 483.152(b)(3).

The skills demonstration must be performed in a facility or laboratory setting comparable to where the aide will work, and administered and evaluated by a registered nurse with at least one year's experience caring for the elderly or chronically ill.

The evaluation may be administered only by the State or a State-approved entity that is not a Medicare skilled nursing facility or Medicaid nursing facility, although a State may allow facility proctoring if the test is secure, standardized and scored externally.
To pass, the aide must pass both parts. A record of success must be entered on the nurse aide registry within 30 days.
An aide who fails must be told which areas were failed and that there are at least three opportunities to take the evaluation.

blocks.text: These are useful design rules for any high-stakes skills assessment. See [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments) and the glossary entry on [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency).

sections.heading: What must a nursing home check before using a nurse aide?

blocks.text: Competence, qualification and registry status. Under 42 CFR 483.35(d)(1), a facility must not use anyone as a nurse aide for more than 4 months, on a full-time basis, unless the person is competent and has completed a state-approved training and competency evaluation program or competency evaluation program, or has been deemed competent. Temporary, per diem and leased aides must meet the same standard from day one under 483.35(d)(2).

items: Registry verification, 483.35(d)(4): before allowing someone to serve as a nurse aide, the facility must receive registry verification that the person has met competency evaluation requirements, unless the person is in an approved program or has recently completed one and is not yet listed, in which case the facility must follow up.
Multi-State checks, 483.35(d)(5): the facility must seek information from every State registry it believes will include information on the individual.

Retraining after a lapse, 483.35(d)(6): if there has been a continuous period of 24 consecutive months without nursing or nursing-related services for pay since the last program, the individual must complete a new training and competency evaluation program or a new competency evaluation program.
Performance review, 483.35(d)(7): every nurse aide needs a performance review at least once every 12 months, and in-service education must be based on the outcome.

blocks.text: Under [42 CFR 483.156](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-483/subpart-D/section-483.156), States must also remove from registry eligibility people who have performed no nursing or nursing-related services for 24 consecutive months, so a lapse can show up both in hiring checks and on the registry itself.

sections.heading: Who approves programs, and who pays?

blocks.text: States approve programs for no more than 2 years at a time and must review a program when it makes substantive changes. A State may not approve a program offered by or in a facility that, in the previous two years, was subject to listed sanctions, such as an extended or partial extended survey or a civil money penalty of not less than $5,000 as adjusted annually, although CMS may waive the disapproval when the penalty was unrelated to quality of care.

Under 483.152(c) and 483.154(c), an aide who is employed by, or has an offer of employment from, a facility on the day the program starts may not be charged for any portion of it, including textbooks. If someone pays and then becomes employed or receives an offer within 12 months of completing the program, the State must provide pro rata reimbursement of costs while they work as a nurse aide.

sections.heading: How can a facility map these rules to survey evidence?

blocks.text: State survey agencies must check during every survey whether the nurse aide requirements of 483.35(c) and (d) and 483.95(g) are met. The table below is an illustrative register for each aide's file. The December 3, 2025 [repeal of the minimum staffing standards](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/03/2025-21792/medicare-and-medicaid-programs-repeal-of-minimum-staffing-standards-for-long-term-care-facilities) did not remove any of these training rules.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each 483.152(b) curriculum area to learning outcomes and to the 483.154 assessment method, written, oral or demonstrated, and links performance review findings to the in-service topics they trigger. This gives a facility one view of whether each aide is qualified, current and within the 24-month window. See [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Is 75 hours the nurse aide training requirement in every state?
faqs.a: 75 clock hours is the federal minimum in 42 CFR 483.152(a)(1) for a state-approved program. States approve programs and may set higher hour requirements, so the hours required in a given state can exceed 75. Check the state's nurse aide program rules as well as the federal floor.

faqs.q: Can a nursing home use an uncertified aide while they train?
faqs.a: For a limited time. 483.35(d)(1) bars using anyone as a nurse aide for more than 4 months full-time unless they are competent and have completed an approved program. 483.35(d)(3) allows an aide with under 4 months in the facility to work if they are a full-time employee in an approved program or have demonstrated competence.

faqs.q: What happens if a nurse aide has not worked for two years?
faqs.a: If there has been a continuous period of 24 consecutive months without providing nursing or nursing-related services for monetary compensation, 483.35(d)(6) requires a new training and competency evaluation program or a new competency evaluation program before the person works as a nurse aide again.

faqs.q: Can a nursing home run the nurse aide competency test itself?
faqs.a: Not as the administering entity. 483.154(c) limits administration and evaluation to the State or a State-approved entity that is not a Medicare or Medicaid nursing facility. A State may allow facility staff to proctor the test if it is secure, standardized and scored by an approved outside organization with no scoring by facility personnel.

faqs.q: Can an aide be charged for nurse aide training?
faqs.a: Not if they are employed by, or have an offer of employment from, a facility on the day the program starts. 483.152(c) bars charging for any portion of the program, including textbooks. Others who become employed within 12 months of completing the program are entitled to pro rata reimbursement through the State.

483.152(b)(1): at least 16 hours on communication, infection control, safety/emergency incl. Heimlich, independence, residents' rights prior to any direct contact; (b)(2)-(7) curriculum; (c) no charges for employed or offered aides, pro rata reimbursement within 12 months.

483.154: choice of written or oral exam from question pool; skills demonstration of random items including all personal care skills; administered by State or approved non-SNF/NF entity; RN with 1 year elderly/chronically ill experience evaluates skills; pass both parts; registry entry within 30 days; at least three opportunities.

483.35(d)(1)-(7): no use as nurse aide more than 4 months full-time unless qualified; non-permanent staff must be qualified; registry and multi-State verification; (d)(6) 24 consecutive months without paid nursing services requires new NATCEP or CEP; (d)(7) performance review every 12 months.
